title: Effects of single and double mutations on the MYC promoter G-quadruplex using a custom G4 DNA microarray: conformational landscape and nearby guanine compensation.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded from NCBI GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) the three series matrices of GSE133368 (0.2/0.6/4.2 MB gzipped) and the 10 MB family SOFT file, which carries the probe tables. On the array the paper used (GPL26850, 'Danzhou_G4'): 15,671 probe IDs, all 60-nucleotide sequences, 14,482 unique, 1,189 duplicate sequences under different IDs, 114 samples, 0 missing cells in the 15,671x114 value matrix, only 4 probes at the 16-bit scanner ceiling on one array. By Hamming distance (number of differing letters) I found 2,146 sequences within 2 mutations of Myc22 wild-type TGAGGGTGGGGAGGGTGGGGAA = 1 wild-type + 66 single + 2,079 double mutants, exactly the paper's 2,145 mutants. I also found three further complete mutation libraries nobody analysed: 3,004 variants of a 26-nucleotide MYC scaffold, 2,146 of a second 22-nucleotide G4, 1,597 of a 19-nucleotide G4, plus all 78 single mutants of the human telomere repeat. I reproduced the paper's headline numbers from the four 0.3 micromolar potassium arrays: position G14 39-47% of wild-type binding (paper 48%), G18 43-50% (52%), G19 41-49% (47%), G8/G11 above wild-type (113-127%). I measured the lithium control arrays (G4 cannot fold in lithium): signal drops to 2-4% of potassium. Technical replicate Spearman within a library: 0.89 (Myc22), 0.92, 0.95, 0.68. I computed the paper's own multiplicative baseline myself: Spearman 0.886 and R-squared 0.744 on the 2,079 Myc22 double mutants.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the microarray probes were printed in 11 replicate copies each and that the deposited value is their median (stated in the GEO processing field and the paper's methods; the per-replicate spreads are not in the processed files). The circular-dichroism and nuclear-magnetic-resonance validation on a handful of individual mutants. Which exact subset of the 44 pyridostatin samples the authors averaged - the paper says only 'extracted from previously described experiments'. The journal supplementary file list: Europe PMC's supplementaryFiles endpoint timed out twice, so Supplementary Table S1 (the sequence-and-value table) was not retrievable; I rebuilt the equivalent table from GEO instead.

a1_downloadable.note: Open NCBI GEO FTP, no login: I downloaded all three series matrices, the 10 MB family SOFT file and the platform annotation. The 517 MB raw-scan tar was left alone (not needed).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The label is the VALUE column of each sample: median fluorescence intensity per target sequence. Sequences come from the platform table on probe ID, a verified one-to-one key. Only extra steps are collapsing 1,189 duplicate sequences and dividing by the wild-type value on the same array.

a3_inputs_present.note: Full 60-nucleotide probe sequences are in the platform table (#SEQUENCE = target sequence); no accession lookups needed.

a4_units_stated.note: GEO states '#VALUE = The median fluorescence intensity of the target sequence'. Units are arbitrary fluorescence counts and the gain differs between arrays (medians 14,029 and 17,894 at high gain versus 3,421 and 4,438 at low gain), so values must be used as ratios within an array - exactly what the paper does.

a5_enough_rows.note: 8,977 mutant sequences in four complete single+double mutation libraries (2,146 + 3,004 + 2,146 + 1,597, counted in the files), inside 14,482 unique array sequences measured under 114 conditions.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Everything needed is 11 MB gzipped text; the feature/label table is under 10 MB. No GPU.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Exact match: 66 single and 2,079 double mutants of Myc22 = 2,145, as claimed, plus wild-type. Platform row count 15,671 matches GEO's declared !Platform_data_row_count.

a8_label_provenance.note: Label is a physical measurement - fluorescence of a Cy5-tagged G4-binding ligand (pyridostatin) bound to DNA on a glass slide - not any model's output, and not computable from the sequence features. Caveat for claims, not for validity: it is a ligand-binding proxy for folding, not a thermodynamic stability value.

B1.why: Two files join cleanly: platform sequence table plus series matrix, on probe ID; verified in the files.

B2.why: Gzipped tab-separated text; my parser read platform table and matrix first try, no malformed rows.

B3.why: One lab, one assay, but two scanner gains across arrays; comparable after dividing by wild-type per array.

B4.why: Verified 0 missing cells in 15,671x114; only 4 probes hit the scanner ceiling on one array.

B5.why: 1,189 duplicate sequences under different probe IDs; collapse by median, trivially.

B6.why: GEO documents every column and the processing, treatment and scan protocols in full.

C1.why: Does mutation-effect prediction transfer to an unseen G4 scaffold? Informative either way; verified 4 scaffolds exist.

C2.why: Many open G4 predictors (DeepG4, G4mismatch, PENGUINN, G4Boost, G4STAB) but none evaluated on within-scaffold mutations.

C3.why: Three of the four complete mutation libraries I found in the files have never been analysed by anyone.

C4.why: Alternative is circular dichroism or nuclear magnetic resonance per sequence; the paper managed only a handful.

C5.why: I computed the paper's multiplicative baseline myself: Spearman 0.886, R-squared 0.744 on Myc22 doubles.

D1.why: Open-weight DNA language models fit 60-nucleotide inputs: HyenaDNA, DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer.

D2.why: 14,482 short sequences; embeddings cache once on a laptop CPU in well under an hour.

D3.why: HyenaDNA/DNABERT-2 permissive; GEO data public domain. Nucleotide Transformer v2 is non-commercial, so avoidable.

E1.why: Leave-one-scaffold-out: group column built by Hamming distance to each wild-type hub; I built it and checked the counts.

E2.why: Five groups: 3,004 / 2,146 / 2,146 / 1,597 variants plus 84 telomere-repeat singles; four are large.

E3.why: Per-scaffold mean, G-count-only rule, G4Hunter score, and the measured multiplicative model (Spearman 0.886).

E4.why: Four technical replicate arrays; replicate Spearman measured at 0.89, 0.92, 0.95 and 0.68 per library.

E5.why: Lithium arrays collapse signal to 2-4% of potassium (verified), and the textbook outer-versus-inner-guanine rule holds (G8 127% vs G14 43%).

E6.why: Label shuffling, constant-tail-only features, nearest-neighbour copy, and G-count-only ablation are all runnable in minutes.

E7.why: Two independent array designs in the same series (2,226 and 18,491 unique sequences) plus a BG4-antibody readout channel.

E8.why: I reproduced the paper's G14/G18/G19 percentages to within ~5 points, and G4mismatch reports 0.81 correlation on this array.

G1.why: Only DNA sequences and array-local probe IDs; genome coordinates must be recovered by sequence alignment.

G2.why: G4-seq genome-wide propensity scores (Chambers et al.) and BG4 ChIP-seq peaks, joinable by sequence for the natural probes.

G3.why: Natural-sequence probes map to the genome cleanly, but engineered mutants have no genomic counterpart at all.

G4.why: Asks whether genome-scale G4 scores reflect real single-base mutation effects - neither dataset answers that alone.

H1.why: Every mutation is reported whether it helps or hurts; range 0.04-2.34 of wild-type; lithium no-fold condition included.

H2.why: One lab, one array platform, one ligand readout, five mostly parallel-type human G4 scaffolds.

H3.why: The claim is writable in one sentence and bounded by what I verified; see honest_claim_h3.

H4.why: Paper states explicitly that fluorescence only approximates stability and that ligand accessibility may vary.

I1.why: Danzhou Yang's G4 drug-design lab (Purdue), the G4mismatch authors, and G4-seq groups; all named.

I2.why: Decides whether promoter-G4 mutation annotation by sequence scores is trustworthy, and which mutants to run by nuclear magnetic resonance next.

I3.why: Ranking metric plus precision in the top 50 disruptive mutants matches the pick-a-few-for-the-bench decision.

I4.why: A two-term multiplicative rule already reaches R-squared 0.74-0.79 within a scaffold, so ML only earns its place across scaffolds.

J1.why: Grouped splits, leakage controls, frozen DNA-language-model embeddings plus a head: real modelling practice.

J2.why: G-run and bulge/vacancy rules are textbook, and the lithium control plus the paper's figures give a sanity check.

J3.why: The assembled 8,977-variant landscape table is useful on its own even if every model fails.

J4.why: Three weeks proposed here (one to the table and baselines, two to models) but not yet written into NOTES.md.

J5.why: Kill condition stated in success_criteria; not yet committed with a date in NOTES.md.

existing_models.name: G4mismatch (deep convolutional network predicting G-quadruplex propensity from G4-seq sequencing data, Barshai & Orenstein, PLOS Computational Biology 2023)
existing_models.score_and_split: Pearson correlation above 0.8 on a held-out human chromosome; reported Pearson 0.81 and 0.78 against the pyridostatin binding intensities of this very microarray's probes (stated in its abstract, which I read in search results, not re-run by me).
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Fine-grained, single-base resolution of G4 propensity and transfer to non-human genomes; the array comparison was made at the coarse G4-versus-non-G4 probe level, not within one scaffold's mutants.

existing_models.name: DeepG4 (convolutional network for cell-type-specific active G-quadruplex regions, Rocher et al., PLOS Computational Biology 2021)
existing_models.score_and_split: AUROC (area under the receiver operating curve) above 0.98 for active G4 regions, on genomic region splits; designed for 200-nucleotide genomic windows, not 22-nucleotide oligos.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Which DNA motifs and chromatin factors make a G4 active in a given cell type; nothing about mutation-level resolution.

existing_models.name: PENGUINN and G4detector (convolutional networks for in vitro G4 regions, 2020-2021)
existing_models.score_and_split: Both report high classification accuracy on G4-seq-derived positive/negative genomic sets; reported as outperformed by DeepG4 and G4Boost.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Distinguishing G4s that actually fold in vivo from sequence alone.

existing_models.name: G4Boost (gradient-boosted trees for G4 folding probability and folding free energy, BMC Bioinformatics 2022)
existing_models.score_and_split: Accuracy above 93%, F1 0.96 for folded/unfolded; R-squared 0.95 and RMSE 4.28 for folding energy, on its own simulated/curated split.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Stability prediction for sequences outside canonical G4 motif patterns.

existing_models.name: G4STAB (multi-input deep network for G4 melting temperature from sequence, salt and pH, Bioinformatics 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on 2,382 diverse DNA G4 sequences with measured melting temperatures; split not verified by me.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Accuracy without hand-coded structural features; generalisation beyond its curated melting-temperature set.

backbone.name: HyenaDNA-tiny or DNABERT-2 (open-weight DNA language models), frozen, with a small regression head; one-hot convolutional network as the sanity baseline
backbone.hardware: 16 GB laptop CPU; 14,482 sequences of 60 nucleotides embed once in well under an hour
backbone.licence: HyenaDNA and DNABERT-2 permissive; data are public-domain NCBI GEO records; Nucleotide Transformer v2 would add a non-commercial clause, so skip it

integration.partner_dataset: G4-seq genome-wide G-quadruplex propensity (mismatch scores, Chambers et al.) and/or precomputed G4mismatch scores; secondarily the BG4-antibody channel already on the same array
integration.join_key: the DNA sequence itself (and genomic coordinate, recovered by alignment, for the probes taken from the human genome)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do genome-scale G-quadruplex propensity scores, which people use to flag cancer promoter mutations, actually track the measured effect of single-base changes on folding?

controls.positive_control: Lithium-chloride arrays, where G-quadruplexes cannot fold: signal falls to 2-4% of potassium (verified). Plus the textbook rule that mutating an outer guanine of a four-guanine run is tolerated while an inner guanine of a three-guanine run is not (verified: G8 127% versus G14 43% of wild-type).
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the binding labels and confirm collapse to the per-scaffold mean; train on the constant 38-nucleotide tail only (must be at chance); nearest-neighbour label copying to show how much a random split would flatter; guanine-count-only ablation.
controls.external_validation: The two other array designs in the same GEO series (2,226 and 18,491 unique sequences, different design and hybridisation batches), the BG4-antibody readout as an independent G4 probe, and published melting-temperature sets (e.g. the 2,382 sequences behind G4STAB).

honest_claim_h3: For sequences one or two mutations away from five human promoter and telomere G-quadruplex scaffolds, a sequence model can rank how much each mutation reduces binding of the G4 ligand pyridostatin on one lab's potassium-buffered DNA microarray - a folding proxy, not a thermodynamic stability measurement - and we can state how much of that ranking survives on a scaffold the model never saw.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a short DNA sequence to predict how much a mutation weakens a four-stranded G-quadruplex structure in a gene promoter.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example is one 22-to-26-letter DNA sequence that differs from a wild-type G-quadruplex by one or two letters, together with the measured brightness of a fluorescent G4-binding drug stuck to it. I counted 8,977 such mutants spanning four complete mutation libraries, inside 14,482 unique array sequences measured under 114 conditions.
plain_idea.predict: The output is the ligand brightness relative to the unmutated sequence on the same array, which is high when the structure still folds. The true value is a median fluorescence reading from a custom Agilent DNA microarray incubated in potassium buffer with Cy5-labelled pyridostatin; lithium-buffered arrays serve as the no-folding control.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups that score cancer mutations in gene promoters for 'destroys a G-quadruplex' rely on genome-wide sequence scores that have never been tested at single-letter resolution; this says whether they can be trusted and which mutants deserve a nuclear-magnetic-resonance experiment next.

more_or_better_data.why: For the specific question of single-base mutation effects inside one G4, the existing models have essentially no training data; this array has 8,977 measured single and double mutants across four scaffolds, counted by me in the files. G4mismatch learned from ~400 million genomic windows, but at coarse genomic resolution and from a different assay; G4STAB from 2,382 melting temperatures.

confidence_score.why: Four technical replicate arrays and two scanner gains let us estimate per-sequence noise (replicate Spearman 0.68-0.95 by library, measured), and lithium arrays give a signal floor - so calibrated uncertainty is possible. But the deposited values are already medians over the 11 printed copies, so the within-array probe spread is lost.

models_beatable.why: DeepG4 (2021), PENGUINN (2020), G4detector (2021) and Quadron are pre-transformer convolutional nets on genomic region splits and are weak at this resolution; G4mismatch (2023) is strong genome-wide on a held-out chromosome and already reports 0.81 correlation with this array's probe intensities, so beating it at its own task is unlikely - beating it at within-scaffold mutation ranking is plausible because no one tried.

guaranteed_improvement.why: G4mismatch can be run as our baseline and our model would see everything it sees, but the new partner data (G4-seq) measures a different quantity by a different assay, and our engineered mutants have no genomic counterpart, so the same-quantity and same-split conditions fail.

label_elsewhere.sources: G4-seq genome-wide mismatch scores for human and other species (known resource, used by G4mismatch); melting-temperature collections behind G4Boost and G4STAB (the latter reports 2,382 G4 sequences, from its abstract found by search); BG4 ChIP-seq and CUT&Tag peak sets; the same GEO series' other two array designs. All are related readouts of G4 formation rather than the same fluorescence measurement.
label_elsewhere.join_key: DNA sequence (and genomic coordinate for natural sequences)
label_elsewhere.why: Other G4 datasets give an external test of whether a model trained on ligand binding predicts folding measured a different way, but none contains the mutant sequences themselves, so they cannot enlarge the training set directly.

risks: Every sequence inside a library differs from its wild-type by at most two letters, so a random split places near-identical sequences in train and test and a nearest-neighbour lookup would score deceptively well.
Each scaffold carries its own fixed 38-letter tail (verified: Myc22's tail differs from Myc26's), so a model can recognise the scaffold from the constant region and simply memorise its average.
Arrays were scanned at two gains (array medians 14,029 and 17,894 versus 3,421 and 4,438), so raw intensity encodes which array a reading came from.
1,189 sequences appear under more than one probe ID and would otherwise straddle the split.
Probe row and column coordinates are in the platform annotation, so slide-position artefacts could correlate with signal if raw per-probe data were used.
leakage_plan.split: Leave-one-scaffold-out on a group column built by Hamming distance to each wild-type hub sequence - I built that column and verified the group sizes (3,004 / 2,146 / 2,146 / 1,597 / 84). Inside a scaffold, additionally hold out all variants touching a given position to test position-level extrapolation.
checks: Shuffle labels and confirm performance drops to the per-scaffold mean.
Train on the constant 38-letter tail alone; anything above chance means scaffold identity is leaking.
Report the nearest-neighbour-copy score under both a random and a scaffold-held-out split, to quantify how much a random split would have flattered the model.
Single-feature ablation on guanine count and on G4Hunter score, to see how much of the signal is trivial.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable: the risks are obvious and the grouping column is cheap to build, but a random split here would generate a high, meaningless number.

success_criteria.metric: Spearman correlation between predicted and measured relative ligand binding on a completely held-out scaffold's double mutants, plus precision among the 50 predicted most-disruptive mutants - because a lab would take about that many to circular dichroism or nuclear magnetic resonance.
success_criteria.baselines: Per-scaffold mean (Spearman 0). G4Hunter and G4mismatch scores, both runnable (G4mismatch reports 0.81 Pearson against this array's probe intensities). The paper's own multiplicative rule, which I measured on the files: Spearman 0.886 / R-squared 0.744 for Myc22 doubles, 0.897/0.789, 0.869/0.740 and 0.758/0.574 for the other three libraries - but it needs the held-out scaffold's 60-80 measured single mutants, so it only applies in the warm-start setting.
success_criteria.success: Cold start (nothing measured on the test scaffold): Spearman >= 0.70 on its double mutants and at least 0.15 above G4mismatch and G4Hunter on the same split. Warm start (test scaffold's singles given): beat the multiplicative rule's 0.886 Spearman on at least three of the four libraries.
success_criteria.kill: If after one week a cold-start model fails to beat G4Hunter by 0.05 Spearman on two held-out scaffolds, stop and publish the benchmark plus the assembled table.

ambitious.why: It publishes G-quadruplex biology and sequence-to-structure predictors; it would take a model that predicts an unseen scaffold's mutation landscape well enough to nominate disruptive mutations that then check out by circular dichroism or nuclear magnetic resonance.

realistic.why: The likely result is a careful benchmark - do genome-wide G4 predictors resolve single-base mutation effects? - plus the first assembled 8,977-variant mutation-landscape table and a frozen-DNA-language-model baseline; that is exactly their application-note and benchmark remit.

fallback.journal: BMC Bioinformatics, or a bioRxiv preprint with a public benchmark repository
fallback.why: Even a flat negative - no existing predictor and no pretrained backbone resolves within-scaffold mutations better than a guanine-count rule - is publishable there alongside the released table and code.

pitch.headline: One public microarray hides four complete single- and double-mutation landscapes of human G-quadruplexes - 8,977 measured variants. The paper analysed one.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Verified in the files: 2,146 Myc22, 3,004 Myc26, 2,146 and 1,597 variants of two further scaffolds; lithium control arrays drop signal to 2-4%; four technical replicates; zero missing cells; all inside 11 MB of public GEO text.
pitch.the_win: A sequence model that ranks a never-seen scaffold's double mutants at Spearman 0.70 or better, where G4Hunter and G4mismatch - the latter reporting 0.81 across this array's diverse probes - have never been tested at single-base resolution.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We learn that genome-wide G4 scores cannot resolve single-base effects, which matters because people use them to flag cancer promoter mutations - and the assembled 8,977-variant table plus the lithium-control benchmark stands on its own.
pitch.who_wants_it: Danzhou Yang's lab (Purdue) choosing which mutants to take to nuclear magnetic resonance; the G4mismatch authors and G4-seq groups needing a single-base calibration set.

ml_idea: Build the feature/label table from GEO GSE133368 design 3: 8,977 single and double mutants across four G-quadruplex scaffolds (plus telomere-repeat singles), each with relative Cy5-pyridostatin binding on four replicate potassium arrays and lithium no-fold controls. Predict relative binding from the 60-nucleotide sequence with (a) a guanine-count/G4Hunter rule, (b) a one-hot convolutional net, (c) a frozen HyenaDNA or DNABERT-2 embedding plus a ridge/gradient-boosting head, under leave-one-scaffold-out grouping. Headline experiment: cold-start transfer to a held-out scaffold, benchmarked against G4Hunter and G4mismatch, with the paper's multiplicative singles rule (Spearman 0.886 measured) as the warm-start ceiling to beat.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not guessed: downloads totalled ~11 MB; my parsing plus all-pairs Hamming-distance scan over 18,451 sequences ran in a few minutes of laptop CPU inside ~2 GB; the full variant table and the multiplicative baseline took one scripting session. Embedding time is an estimate for 14,482 sequences of 60 nucleotides through a small DNA language model on CPU.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Already done, and it reshaped the project: count the complete mutation libraries on the array and score the two-term multiplicative rule. There are four libraries (8,977 variants), and the rule already reaches R-squared 0.74-0.79 within a scaffold - so the within-scaffold task is nearly solved and the project only survives as a cross-scaffold transfer benchmark. Next cheapest check: run G4Hunter on all 8,977 variants and see whether it correlates at all.

verdict_reason: Every Part A item was verified in the downloaded files, including an exact count match (66 singles + 2,079 doubles = the paper's 2,145) and reproduction of the paper's headline percentages to within about five points. The payoff is that the array holds three more complete mutation libraries nobody has analysed, giving 8,977 labelled variants, five hold-out groups, a built-in lithium negative control and four technical replicates in 11 MB of text. The honest framing is a transfer benchmark plus a new resource table, not a new state-of-the-art G4 predictor: within a scaffold the space is exhaustively measured and a two-term multiplicative rule already reaches R-squared 0.74-0.79, so the question worth asking is whether anything - a pretrained DNA language model or an existing genome-wide predictor - generalises to a scaffold it never saw.
